title: From Records to Streaming
objective: After this level you can explain how music moved from records to MP3s to streaming.
summary: The CD (1982) samples 44,100 times a second to cover hearing up to 20 kHz; MP3 drops what you can't hear; streaming made up 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025.

cards.headline: In 2025, 82% of US recorded-music money came from streaming.
cards.body: That's the Recording Industry Association of America's count, measured at wholesale. Getting from discs on a shelf to songs that arrive through a phone took three big ideas.

cards.headline: Idea 1: turn sound into numbers
cards.body: Sony and Philips brought the compact disc to market in 1982. A CD stores sound as digital data, microscopic pits and flat spots read by a laser. It measures the sound wave 44,100 times every second. Why so many? To capture a frequency, you must sample more than twice as often, and remember Level 3: hearing tops out around 20 kHz. Twice that is 40,000, and the CD adds a little headroom.

cards.headline: Idea 2: throw away what you can't hear
cards.body: Researchers at Germany's Fraunhofer institute found a shortcut: store the parts of a sound your ear can't perceive with less precision. Their MP3 files came out up to ten times smaller, with virtually no audible difference. The team chose the name ".mp3" by email poll on July 14, 1995. In 1999, college student Shawn Fanning's Napster let people share music files over the internet, until a court fight with the record industry shut it down in 2001.

cards.headline: Idea 3: stream it, don't store it
cards.body: Spotify, founded in Sweden, launched in 2008 and streamed songs instead of selling files: free with ads, or paid without them. That model won. The RIAA put streaming at 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025. Discs, then files, then streams: each step made music lighter to carry, until it weighed nothing at all.

mascot.line: From a shelf of discs to a phone in your pocket, in about four decades.
